item.title: Album of the Week: Midnite Vultures by Beck
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: The darling of 90’s alternative, Beck has always had an obvious weird streak (I’m talking musically, not just because he’s a Scientologist). Before Loser catapulted him to superstardom, his earlier work can best be described as backcountry grunge blues with heavy doses of pure noise. Watching him harness his creative powers into more listenable avenues [...]
item.content:encoded:
The darling of 90’s alternative, Beck has always had an obvious weird streak (I’m talking musically, not just because he’s a Scientologist).  Before Loser catapulted him to superstardom, his earlier work can best be described as backcountry grunge blues with heavy doses of pure noise.  Watching him harness his creative powers into more listenable avenues resulted in two absolute gems of an album on Odelay and Mutations, the first going commercial gangbusters and giving him plenty of dough to just goof around.  And goof around he did on the follow-up Midnite Vultures, it’s lots of fun, it’s varied but it’s also downright strange.

For someone known as an alt-rocker to make a full-on electro-funk turn would be a lot more common these days, but at the time it was really something.  There’s plenty of horn sections, upbeat rhythms, sometimes out-and-out electronic synth clanging and thumping, and all-in-all never a dull moment.  When it came out a lot of people were put off coming to expect more “Beck” tracks, and it was panned as porn funk to the point Beck even came out after its release saying he hated the album.  I hope in hindsight he’s changed his mind, because I sure as hell still love it, and it’s an amazingly singular mark in his 10+ album catalogue for being different.  It was even nominated for the Album of the Year Grammy in 2001, not that I put much stock in that.

Rather than going through it track by track, I’ll just say all the songs are great in their own way, except Hollywood Freaks.  Dear God that song is awful, Beck should stay away from lazy gangsta lean rap.  But while the album starts off upbeat and in your face with Sexx Laws and Nicotine & Gravy, I think a lot of the beauty in the album comes from the lyrics, which is something I rarely say.  Yes, the songs are all catchy and well-produced otherwise it wouldn’t suit my tastes, but I can’t think of many other albums with as many head-turning “wait, did he just say that??” moments.  This could be the result of Beck letting loose his weirdness in all its over-the-top tongue-in-cheek splendour, or it could be the result of rising to celebrity status and having way too much sex, but either way it’s great for several laughs.

Gems scattered throughout Midnite Vultures include “let the handcuffs slip off your wrist, I’ll let you be my chaperone”…“I’ll do your laundry, massage your soul”…“it’s Thursday night, I think I’m pregnant again”…“you look good in that sweater and aluminum crutch”…”I wanna get with you, only you girl, and your sister, I think her name is Debra”…the list continues.  That last one is from the closer track Debra, which is about as cheesy as it gets, and correspondingly one of the best and most hilarious tracks on the album.  It drags on, but in a positive way for effect, only to break into minutes of silence and then the bonus track, which you really need to watch out for because it’s grating noise for no reason other than, well, it’s Beck.

You can pick this album up at Amazon

Or iTunes

item.title: Phoenix NASCAR Subway 500
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Nothing’s more American than NASCAR, beer and hot dogs. Rolling into Phoenix for the Subway Fresh Fit 500, I met up with one of my many connects across the country and managed to snag a $400 all access pit hot pass. So as you can see from the gallery, I was able to get up [...]
item.content:encoded:
Nothing’s more American than NASCAR, beer and hot dogs.  Rolling into Phoenix for the Subway Fresh Fit 500, I met up with one of my many connects across the country and managed to snag a $400 all access pit hot pass.  So as you can see from the gallery, I was able to get up close and personal with the cars in the garage, stand on pit road during the race and pretend I knew what I was doing to get into the professional photographer only area on turn 1 for some great shots during the race.  It was a little daunting at first trying to not get run over or get in the way of pit crew folks rolling around tires and fuel canisters, but I got the hang of it pretty quick and didn’t get yelled at once all weekend!

Right there in the pits

Also, for you folks reading at home, I changed the site a little bit so you can click on one thumbnail to get the blown up version, then just cycle through all of them, should make it a little easier to navigate.  It’s something called lightbox, and even facebook switched to using it recently, so I may as well get on board.

While watching souped up cars driving around in circles isn’t really my thing, it’s certainly something worth doing once, if only just to observe your typical NASCAR fan.  Being in the pits I got more of the white trash with money crowd, but I was still able to see a missing teeth, camo wearing bearded fat guy yelling at his children while swilling a beer and overhear someone criticizing the pole sitter of the race for being an atheist.  Rookie Trevor Bayne who won the Daytona 500 the week prior is a bible thumper, so huge with the fans, and the media was all over his jock all week.  He’s only 20 so I’ll root for the kid too, but after wrecking in practice he managed the same feat during the race only 20 laps in.

Zoom zoom

The race itself was a giant mess, only half the cars in the field finished, there was even a full blown red flag where everyone had to just stop in the middle of the track to clean up all the smashed car bits.  In the end Jeff Gordon wound up winning his first race in over 2 years, and you could tell all day his car was just faster.  Hanging out with the race engineers for the RCR team (Richard Childress Racing with drivers Jeff Burton, Kevin Harvick and Paul Menard) I learned that while the good ol’ boy mentality of the sport still prevails, they’re slowly switching over to a more scientific perspective.  A lot of talk of wing, camber, spring stiffness and tire pressure was over my head, but it’s neat to see the delicate balance and learn that the engineers job isn’t just to make the car as fast as a 3D computer simulation will allow on a given track, they actually described that as only 40% of the battle, the other 60% being to listen to the driver and get the car to respond to his particular racing style.

Hehehe

While many of the drivers are derided as prima donnas who aren’t held accountable, I got to meet Paul Menard and he was a nice guy who actually introduced himself to me and shook my hand.  I suppose I was in his trailer and maybe he wanted to be nice so I wouldn’t touch anything, but I hear he’s a down to earth guy.

A lot of the real magic is in the sound and motion, and I have about 30 different clips of footage I need to edit together (ohh right, the Youtube from the pits!), but that’s not exactly a priority right now and having never edited a video before, perhaps not the best use of my time when I’m getting ready to drive back to Quartzsite again to sit in the middle of the desert.  In the meantime, check the gallery.

item.title: Just Another Day at the Office in Quartzsite AZ
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: What bothers me is that I actually have a plan and I’m executing it. Two weeks ago I said I needed to go park in the middle of the desert away from any distractions and be productive, and here I am. Even at the time I wavered, contemplating robbing banks or selling drugs as I’ve [...]
item.content:encoded:
What bothers me is that I actually have a plan and I’m executing it.  Two weeks ago I said I needed to go park in the middle of the desert away from any distractions and be productive, and here I am.  Even at the time I wavered, contemplating robbing banks or selling drugs as I’ve always joked, but unfortunately no.  For five days I’ve been camped out on BLM lands 6 miles south of Quartzsite AZ…working.

My office in Quartzsite AZ

I haven’t moved more than 10 yards in that timeframe, I haven’t spoken to a soul, I certainly haven’t showered or shaved.  I eat and drink the food and water I packed in, I harvest the energy of the sun to power my laptop tethered to my phone to access the internet to hock various products on various websites in what are but the crude, malnourished saplings of “internet business”.  It’s a necessary evil, but being the first time I’ve done such “work” for personal commercial gain in oh, a year, it obviously makes me hearken back to the good ol’ days which I jokingly refer to with new acquaintances I meet on the road as “when I used to be a normal person”.  As you can well imagine, I take stock of what lines illicit the best response after telling my story about a hundred times, and that one ranks quite highly.

Problem is, the old necessary evil had no beginning or end, no means or justification.  This evil is mine and mine alone, so I can just put it on pause, drive to from Quartzsite AZ to Phoenix AZ and party.  But Phoenix scares me, all I can picture is old people, mega malls, firearms and Christianity.  It is but two hours away and I will likely drive there Thursday to watch my NASCAR and spring training baseball (as also foreshadowed), then turn around and return to the desert.

Tell me that rock doesn't look like an 18th century lady serving tea

Realizations, several of them occur rapid fire now that I have nothing but time to think, and I welcome it.  One, I need but $12000 a year to maintain this lifestyle.  Self-employed or not, think what amount of effort you would need to procure that amount of money yourself.  Hopefully the answer is minimal.  Two, $12000 a year is right on the so-called poverty line, yet in my mind I live like a king.  Three, I once had visions, aspirations that I could yell these things at people that they could do it too themselves and be free, to which I now fully understand they would respond “free to live in a van, alone in the middle of the desert?”  And they would be correct.  Perhaps I am uniquely adapted, or perhaps it is a grotesque mutation as they are often one in the same.

You know what, scratch that, you should probably quit your job and be free to live in a van in the middle of the desert.  At least I didn’t yell that.

item.title: Joshua Tree Camping
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I wouldn’t call it Joshua Tree camping so much as Joshua Tree surviving. With so many miles of vast and pristine desert wilderness (as pictured in the gallery) you’d better be prepared for coyotes wandering through your campsite lured by the lamb shanks you’re cooking in the open fire, not to mention rattlesnakes, scorpions and [...]
item.content:encoded:
I wouldn’t call it Joshua Tree camping so much as Joshua Tree surviving.  With so many miles of vast and pristine desert wilderness (as pictured in the gallery) you’d better be prepared for coyotes wandering through your campsite lured by the lamb shanks you’re cooking in the open fire, not to mention rattlesnakes, scorpions and tarantulas, although I was lucky enough to only come across the first creature, and he was nothing but curious.  There is no water or electricity at any of the 10 official Joshua Tree camping grounds so you best pack that in yourself.  Cell phone reception or internet you can totally forget, which explains why I was incommunicado the last 5 days.

The views are unreal

I wouldn’t have even noticed the coyote while I was tending to the fire if it wasn’t for my Quebecois friend Raphael from Trois Riviere.  Having rolled in around 4 PM to Hidden Valley campground, the first one you hit from the main north entrance, I saw the sign read FULL, so did a quick survey, saw nothing and wound up staying the night at Ryan.  I wizened up the next day at noon when I drove back into Hidden Valley to scope the first open spot that it’s more just because the rangers only come by to flip the sign every few days.  There were plenty available so I grabbed an absolutely stunning spot nestled in with some boulders and a view across the expansive desert behind me.

Stunning Barker Dam

After doing the two nearby day hikes of the visually mind boggling Barker Dam and drastically less interesting Wall Street Mill, I was already afraid someone would steal my spot so to return and find a bunch of water and camping gear hidden in the rocks was somewhat disconcerting.  It turned out to be no problem at all though as it was just Raphael’s stuff and had been there all along.

He had a great trick of just pitching his tent in amongst the boulders and staying there for free having hitched into camp from Palm Springs after taking the bus there from Vancouver.  Joshua Tree happens to be one of the climbing meccas of North America with its huge array of varying sizes and difficulties of boulders to scramble up, and Raphael had been doing just that for a full month.  To hear he only spent $250 during that entire stretch definitely put me to shame, but he ate Ramen noodles and canned tuna while I feasted on lamb, corn, roasted red pepper and whiskey, so I’ll take my monetary licks any day.

The Wild West

Raphael had it figured out for sure.  Beyond his tips on the wisdom of not really having to pay because the rangers never came by and screw it because the place was free when he first came 8 years ago before the California budget crisis, he also well understood this fabled “work-life balance”.  Six months a year he cycles through Europe and climbs here or in Red Rocks, the other six months he does seasonal work like picking cherries in the Okanagan and king crab fishing in Alaska.  Naturally I am told it’s nothing at all like the TV show, they work at most 6 hours a day while living on the beach in July.

As for the park itself, I am torn whether it is actually better than the redwoods in terms of nature and is perhaps the first place of my entire trip I will tell people “you have to go here”.  If you’re anywhere near LA, it’s only 2 hours away and more than worth the trip.  Everything feels like a scene out of a Clint Eastwood spaghetti western, or to modernize it, Red Dead Redemption (this is the best video game of all time FYI, if you haven’t played it, get it).

Freaky deaky trees

Wait, I totally just ruined it even trying to compare the place to anything, because there’s really nothing like it.  The Joshua trees themselves just blend into the atmosphere after awhile because the place is so much more than that.  They were gifted their name by Mormon settlers who saw the branches extended to the heavens so naturally gave them a good old fashioned biblical name, but even I could feel the obvious spirituality of the place.  A fellow next to me on the peak of Ryan Mountain exclaimed he felt like he was at the center of the universe.  He also happened to be from Vancouver and a Canucks fan, so his quip about the Calgary Flames almost landed him an express ticket to said spiritual heavens via a more direct route down the side of the mountain with a helpful push from yours truly.

Uhhh…too much to say, check out the gallery, it’s definitely my best yet.

Addendum of interesting facts:

Wild rock formations

-100 years ago it rained twice as much here as it does now.  When I heard about pioneers raising cattle I scoffed at them as insane, but things change and it once actually made sense, although I can’t think of a more desolate, frightening place to live unless I had a ranch with about a dozen people on it.

-A process occurs in the soil here to reverse erosion caused by cryptobiotic bacteria that actually bond sand back together again into a crust.

-Most of the good stuff is in the high desert at the north end of the park, but if you want free Joshua Tree camping (other than the ol’ not paying trick) there’s free BLM lands you can park an RV or pitch a tent on directly outside the south entrance within sight of sign.  Backcountry tent camping is also allowed for free almost anywhere in the park as long as you’re 1 mile from the road and register your vehicle.

item.content:encoded:
No really, check out the guide in the tourist info center, or even their website.  I liked the vibe of the place with everything moving a lot slower than LA, it’s a lot smaller than you’d think, I’m just saying that if I liked dudes I would have stuck around longer.

The town is a strange mix of upscale, and not

Halfway through my typical mid-afternoon stroll through a new town I went to my standard fall back, looking at the Happy Hour app on my phone (I made the mistake of checking recently and found out I use this app more than any other).  Seeing a place called Hunter’s with a strip of three other bars on Arenas Road, I turned the corner and immediately knew what I was getting myself into.  Rainbow flags everywhere, and sure, this is California, you’ll see them in regular places just to show the business isn’t discriminating to customers, but when they’re on every store on the block it’s a bit more apparent.  It’s also the first place I saw a US flag with the stars and stripes replaced with a rainbow, I can’t wait to see what people in Oklahoma have to think about that.

Sidling up to the bar to order my $1.50 Bud Light, I am dismayed to find Hunter’s doesn’t have a kitchen, so my visit will be brief.  Anxious to keep my business, the bartender assures me the place will be hopping in an hour once people start getting off work, and they open the dance floor early because it’s bear night.  He calls me “sweetheart” a few times during the conversation, I eat some free chips and salsa on the patio and am off.

Interesting architecture

Not 10 minutes later some 60 year old Mexican woman stops me on the street, tells me she likes the way I dress, that she is a widow and I should come back to her place.  Politely declining because she was about 5’3”, over 200 lbs and missing a few teeth, I let my Happy Hour app lead me to another spot, this time with food guaranteed as one of the specials is free appetizers.  Somewhere in the midst of disengaging my Mexican lady friend she also informs me that her daughter is an American citizen and single, but the call of free appies is much stronger.

O’Learys is a prettied up dive bar, but the second I walk in a large steaming tray of huge, saucy buffalo wings is placed at a table with napkins and ranch sauce.  The woman behind the bar tells me to help myself after serving me a $2 PRB pint (I paid $4 for a bottle in LA) and tells me she is from Vancouver Island after getting my TD Canada Trust credit card to open up a tab.  A few minutes later another older lady in the bar starts chatting with me because of my camera (it’s a great conversation starter with complete strangers) and tells me she is from Vancouver Island.  Surprised, I start telling her that I just…

“Yup, that’s my sister!  We always come here on Friday night, she gives us free drinks!”  Ahhh, to be in a small town again.

Oh, and check the gallery.

item.title: Mo’ Macro, Mo’ Problems
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I guess I’m doing well if these are my only problems. And they make for a hell of a gallery. Problem 1: Everything is a macro shot Put a macro lens on your camera (or in my case the kit lens with a Canon Extension Tube as explained previously) and you’ll want to take pictures [...]
item.content:encoded:
I guess I’m doing well if these are my only problems.  And they make for a hell of a gallery.

Problem 1: Everything is a macro shot

Put a macro lens on your camera (or in my case the kit lens with a Canon Extension Tube as explained previously) and you’ll want to take pictures of anything you can find.  Bottle caps, cigarette butts, rotting fruit, it’s all fair game.  I still haven’t gotten past the “woah, that’s cool” phase, but hopefully the charm will wear off soon enough so pedestrians aren’t wondering what I’m doing taking pictures of dirt while sitting in a flower bush.

Problem 2: Lens fever

A common SLR photographer problem, I spent four hours yesterday looking at lenses I could never afford wanting several of them.  Yeah, my Canon Extension Tube job for $80 works pretty damn well, but if I bought a $600 macro lens think how sharp they’d be!  And I wouldn’t need to be 2 inches away from the subject.  Then if I got one that was long enough to do telephoto too I could get a tele-extender and…d’oh!  Livin’ in a van guy budget.

Problem 3: The sticky green is too awesome

In what I’m pretty sure is my first pre-planned shot of the entire trip, a friend suggested I try my macro tricks on the sticky icky.  While definitely not the greatest shot, if I could get the right lighting and a tripod rigged up, High Times Magazine here we come.  They’re nifty looking lil’ buggers up close, eh?  And delicious too.  So, so delicious.

Problem 4: I should be doing real work

This is an affliction that has just started hitting me during the last week.  I could wander around shooting photos, drinking beer and indulging problem 3 all the freaking time, then two years from now I’d be completely screwed in life.  I can actually do a solid 6 hours of work now without burning out, and while there’s no need to ramp it all the way up to a crazy 8 hours, I do feel the need to go park somewhere in the middle of the Arizona desert (perhaps Quartzite) and start hammering away at some other projects.
